title: Anthropic's New Open-Source Tool Catches Fake AI APIs Red-Handed!
summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team released FlashProve, an open-source zkSNARK prototype that mathematically verifies whether an API response was generated by a committed set of model weights without revealing the proprietary weights. Tested on Meta's 400B Llama 4 Maverick model on a single H100 GPU, it achieves a 5,500x proving speedup over previous benchmarks and verifies proofs in 17 seconds on a standard CPU.
raw_text: So check this out—have you ever wondered if an AI API provider is secretly swapping out the expensive frontier model you paid for with a cheap, heavily quantized version behind the scenes? Until now, we basically just had to trust them, right? Well, Anthropic's Frontier Red Team just dropped an open-source project called FlashProve, and for developers, this is super interesting. It uses zero-knowledge proofs—specifically zkSNARKs—to mathematically prove that an API response actually came from the exact model weights promised, without the company having to expose their secret weights. Here's the wild part: the previous benchmark on Meta's 400-billion-parameter Llama 4 Maverick took over 14 hours to prove a thousand tokens and created a massive 93-gigabyte proof file. FlashProve does it 5,500 times faster on a single H100 GPU, shrinking the proof down to just under 19 megabytes so your CPU can verify it in 17 seconds. Now, I'll be real with you, it still takes 70 to 95 times more GPU compute than normal inference, so it's strictly a research prototype for now, but verifiable AI is officially becoming a reality.

title: Sub-1-Bit AI Compression?! How LoopVQ Makes Small Models 6x Faster
summary: Researchers at Seoul National University introduced LoopVQ, a quantization method that compresses the KV cache of looped transformers down to 0.5 and 0.25 bits per element. Deployed in the SGLang engine at a 32K context length, the technique nearly halves decode latency and boosts peak serving throughput by up to 6.1x while preserving baseline accuracy.
raw_text: If you follow the technical side of LLM architecture, you probably know about looped transformers like Ouro and Huginn. They reuse the same layer weights across multiple loops to punch way above their weight class. But there has been a massive catch: every single loop step has to store its own KV cache, which eats up memory so fast that the cache actually outgrows the model weights themselves. Well, researchers Minsoo Cheong and Sungjoo Yoo at Seoul National University just published a paper on LoopVQ that solves this bottleneck. Here's what we need to pay attention to: instead of just compressing along standard token or channel axes, they quantized across the loop axis itself, pushing the KV cache down to an ultra-tiny 0.5 or even 0.25 bits per element. Normally, going under 1 bit destroys a model's brain, right? Not here. In SGLang at a 32K context window, LoopVQ kept near-baseline accuracy on complex reasoning while cutting decode latency in half and boosting serving throughput by up to 6.1x. It's a huge win for making compact, looped models actually practical in production.

title: Anthropic's Claude Just Found a Terrifying Cloud Bug That Breaks Virtual Machines!
summary: The Xen Project disclosed two critical vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704) discovered by Anthropic researchers using the Claude AI model. The memory permission-caching flaw allows a malicious guest virtual machine to escape hardware isolation and read or write memory across other VMs and the root host domain.
raw_text: So check this out—if you still think AI models are just glorified autocomplete that can't find deep, complex bugs in hardcore system code, Anthropic's Claude just proved you wrong. The Xen Project just dropped an urgent security advisory for two critical vulnerabilities—XSA-523—and guess who found them? Anthropic researchers using Claude! Now, if you aren't familiar with Xen, it is a foundational open-source hypervisor that keeps virtual machines isolated from each other on cloud servers and security-focused operating systems like Qubes OS. Here's the wild part: Claude spotted a super subtle flaw in how Xen caches memory permissions during batch copy operations. Because Xen skipped re-checking permissions in a weird edge case, an attacker inside one virtual machine could completely break out of hardware isolation and read or write memory across every other VM on the physical server, including the master root domain! There is zero workaround other than patching and rebooting immediately. Between Google's Gemini 4 Carbon and now Claude hunting down hypervisor zero-days, AI cybersecurity is officially in a whole new league.
